title: How Sea Monsters Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore sea monsters across history and culture. They open with pop-culture banter about Sid and Marty Krofft shows and the Montauk Monster (2008, a decomposed raccoon), the East River Monster (a pig), and a 2006 Russian beluga carcass. They argue the sea hides unknown creatures and that science has replaced superstition, citing the anglerfish, the megamouth shark, and deep-sea exploration. Ancient myths follow: Tiamat in Mesopotamia, the Leviathan in the Bible, Chinese dragons, Scylla and Charybdis in the Odyssey, Cetus and Perseus in the Andromeda myth, and the Norse Jormungandr. They discuss theories for where sea monsters came from: allegory and warning tales (including nuclear semiotics and the nuclear priesthood idea), misread real animals (the kraken as giant squid, sea serpents as oarfish, kelpies and mermaids), and dinosaur or fossil finds (Nessie and plesiosaur bones, Chinese dragon bones, the Lakota and Dakota Sioux Unhcegila, and the Cyclops from elephant skulls). Later they cover early naturalist transitional-era maps, the sea bishop (Bishop fish), and whale-island legends. The episode closes with listener mail about a sixteen-foot hammerhead shark pulled into a rowboat by Coast Guard sailors, and a shout-out to Wendy and Rachel.
topics: Jules Verne Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

entities.name: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

segments.title: Opening banter and Sid and Marty Krofft
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Sigmund the Sea Monster and Sid and Marty Krofft, then introduce the sea monster theme and the idea that people have been seeing sea monsters for millennia.

segments.title: Modern sea monster sightings
segments.summary: The Montauk Monster of 2008, a decomposed raccoon, the East River Monster, a pig, and a 2006 Russian beluga carcass are discussed as examples of sensational naming of washed-up carcasses.

segments.title: Unknown ocean life and science replacing superstition
segments.summary: The seas cover most of Earth's surface and hide unknown life. The hosts argue science has replaced superstition, citing the anglerfish footage, the megamouth shark, and deep-sea exploration by James Cameron.

segments.title: Mesopotamian and Biblical sea monsters
segments.summary: Tiamat was originally a benevolent creator goddess before becoming a chaos monster slain by a hero. The hosts also discuss the Leviathan in the Old Testament and possible links to Tiamat.

segments.title: Jules Verne and Greek myths of Cetus and Perseus
segments.summary: Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea is quoted on undiscovered species. The hosts then retell the Greek myth in which Cetus is sent against Andromeda and Perseus kills it.
topics: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

segments.title: Scylla, Charybdis and nuclear semiotics
segments.summary: Scylla and Charybdis from the Odyssey are discussed as possible allegories for a reef and whirlpools. The hosts explain nuclear semiotics and the nuclear priesthood idea of using folklore to warn people away from nuclear waste.

segments.title: Kraken, giant squid and sea serpents
segments.summary: The kraken is likely a giant squid, misread by sailors, and the Norse Jormungandr is discussed. Oarfish are proposed as the basis of sea serpent sightings. Mermaids, kelpies and the Loch Ness Monster are covered, including the plesiosaur-bone link to Nessie.

segments.title: Dinosaur bones and other fossil-based legends
segments.summary: Fossils are linked to monster legends: Chinese dragon bones, the Unhcegila of the Lakota and Dakota Sioux, and the Cyclops from elephant skulls. Early naturalists' transitional era and the sea bishop are also discussed.

segments.title: Listener mail: hammerhead shark and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener's great-grandfather and Coast Guard crew pulled a stunned sixteen-foot hammerhead shark into their rowboat after a dynamite blast. The hosts thank Wendy and Rachel and wish listeners a happy new year.
